title: Carprice Williams: Philadelphia foster mother charged with murder in death of 10-year-old found in a trunk | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The foster mother of a 10-year-old girl, whose disappearance sparked a massive search before her body was found across state lines nearly two weeks later, has been charged with murder, Philadelphia officials said Thursday.

Malayshia Alford was last seen alive at her home in West Philadelphia on October 22. Four days later, she was reported missing, triggering an intense search by locals, the police department and the FBI.

On Wednesday, her body was found in the trunk of a car around 20 miles away in New Jersey after a turning point in the case: video surveillance was obtained from the early morning hours of October 26 showing what authorities believed to be her body being moved out of the home in a bag, Philadelphia Assistant District Attorney Ashley Toczylowski said at a news conference Thursday.

The video pointed police to a witness who ultimately led them to Malayshia’s body in Lindenwold, New Jersey, Toczylowski said. Her cause of death is believed to be blunt force trauma and her manner of death was ruled a homicide, officials said.

“We do have an indication that there were instances of abuse happening, and that items were used to carry out that abuse,” Toczylowski said.

Malayshia’s foster mother, 36-year-old Carprice Williams, has been charged with murder, endangering the welfare of a child, criminal use of a communication facility, possession of an instrument of crime, recklessly endangering another person, tampering with evidence and abuse of a corpse, Toczylowski said. Philadelphia District Attorney Lawrence Krasner previously provided a different spelling of Williams’ first name.

Williams did not have a criminal record, according to Krasner. The Defender Association of Philadelphia, which is representing Williams, declined to comment on the case.

She is being held without bail at the Detention Center in Philadelphia, jail and court records show. Williams, who was arraigned early Friday morning, has a preliminary hearing set for November 23.

Officials in Pennsylvania’s largest city spoke out about the 10-year-old’s killing, including Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin J. Bethel, who said Malayshia “deserved safety. She deserved to be loved. She deserved a chance to grow up.”

Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle L. Parkersaid authorities will continue to investigate the tragedy and seek justice.

“As a mother, this has shaken me to my core,” Parker said in a statement. “I can’t stop thinking about this precious baby and the heartache and turmoil that her immediate village will endure.”

Malayshia was a student at Robert E. Lamberton School, the School District of Philadelphia said.

When Williams reported Malayshia as missing, she told police the girl didn’t return home from school and wasn’t answering her phone, prosecutors said Thursday.

Authorities say they believe Malayshia was removed from Williams’ home after she was last seen there on October 22. The girl was then placed in one car and later transferred to another, Toczylowski said.

Police, the FBI and the community scrambled to find the missing girl. Wayne Jacobs, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Philadelphia, said the “around-the-clock effort” included witness interviews and a review of digital evidence.

The surveillance video recovered Wednesday then eventually led to the grim discovery.

“It was that video that then led law enforcement officials to a suspect vehicle, which then led law enforcement officials to find that vehicle and find a person that they wanted to speak to related to that vehicle,” Toczylowski said.

That witness was interviewed by police and the FBI, which “ultimately led law enforcement officials to her body.”

The charges against Williams are a result of the discovery and “what this witness said to law enforcement,” Toczylowski said.

When Malayshia’s body was found around 11 p.m. Wednesday “it was immediately apparent that she had been there for a while,” Toczylowski said.

Krasner said his office will be in touch with the Philadelphia Department of Human Services, the county’s child welfare agency, and they “look forward to speaking to them further about this.”

The city’s department of human services said Malayshia was in the agency’s custody, noting she was receiving foster care services through Pennsylvania Mentor and case management services from Catholic Community Services, Community Umbrella Agency 4.

“We are incredibly saddened to learn of the death of Malayshia Alford. We offer our sincere condolences to the family on this tragic loss,” Kimberly Ali, the department’s commissioner, said in a statement.

Pennsylvania Mentor is fully cooperating with law enforcement on the matter, but the organization couldn’t comment further due to the ongoing investigation, a spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

“We are heartbroken about the tragic passing of Malayshia Alford, and our thoughts are with Malayshia’s family and friends, her community, and her loved ones during this difficult time,” the Pennsylvania Mentor spokesperson said.

Malayshia’s family expressed their grief at the news conference, saying they loved her and are going through a “very hard time.”

“We appreciate the many prayers and countless hours of searching for our loved one. This is so hard to digest,” said Marketa Brown, Malayshia’s aunt.

As the girl’s family prepares to lay her to rest, Brown said they also thank the outpouring of love and concern from neighbors and community members, many of whom placed pink balloons and teddy bears in front of a memorial honoring Malayshia.

The Rev. Alyn E. Waller, senior pastor of Philadelphia’s Enon Tabernacle Baptist Church, said the community will continue to come together to support Malayshia’s family “to let them know that they are not alone.”

“We are judged by how the children of our community fare,” Waller said in a statement. “Until we can say the children are fine, we are not fine.”

This story has been updated with more information.
